claim: In-gel tryptic digestion followed by MALDI-TOF/TOF analysis identified the 130 kDa CSPG as an N-terminal portion of NCAN.
source: In-gel tryptic digestion followed by a MALDI-TOF/TOF analysis identified the 130 kDa CSPG as an N-terminal portion NCAN (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Figure 1c.

claim: Full-length >250 kDa NCAN is cleaved to generate the N-terminal 130 kDa fragment and C-terminal 150 kDa fragment.
source: Full-length >250 kDa NCAN is reportedly cleaved to generate the N-terminal 130 kDa fragment and C-terminal 150 kDa fragment (Figure 1d; Rauch et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rauch et al., 1992 and illustrated in Figure 1d.

claim: Full-length and N-terminal fragment of NCAN are both detected in the developing cerebral cortex.
source: Using an antibody to the N-terminal portion of NCAN, we found that the full-length and the N-terminal fragment of NCAN were both detected in the developing cerebral cortex (Figure 1e and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 1e and 1f.

claim: Only the cleaved fragment of NCAN is detected in the adult cerebral cortex.
source: In contrast, only the cleaved fragment was detected in the adult cerebral cortex, indicating the developmental stage-dependent proteolytic processing of NCAN (Figure 1e and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 1e and 1f.

claim: NCAN exhibits developmental stage-dependent proteolytic processing.
source: In contrast, only the cleaved fragment was detected in the adult cerebral cortex, indicating the developmental stage-dependent proteolytic processing of NCAN (Figure 1e and f).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential detection of NCAN forms at different developmental stages shown in Figures 1e and 1f.

claim: Ncan mRNA expression is high during late embryonic and early postnatal stages.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR analysis showed high expression levels of Ncan during the late embryonic and early postnatal stages (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Developing cortical neurons secrete full-length and N-terminal fragment of NCAN into the culture medium.
source: The full-length and the N-terminal fragment of NCAN were gradually secreted into the culture medium (Figure 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis of culture medium shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Ncan mRNA expression increases 2 days after GFP labeling of radial glial cells and is thereafter maintained.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR analysis of GFP-positive cells isolated 0.6, 1, 2, and 4 days after labeling demonstrated that Ncan mRNA expression increased 2 days after labeling and was thereafter maintained (Figure 1j).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1j.

claim: Developing cortical neurons express Ncan mRNA and are capable of secreting NCAN.
source: These results indicated that developing cortical neurons themselves express Ncan mRNA and are capable of secreting NCAN.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of in utero labeling and RT-PCR analysis.

claim: Ncan mRNA is widely distributed throughout the developing cerebral cortex.
source: The widespread distribution of Ncan mRNA throughout the cerebral cortex indicated that NCAN production involves developing neurons as well as other cell populations, including radial glial cells (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: NCAN production involves developing neurons as well as other cell populations, including radial glial cells.
source: The widespread distribution of Ncan mRNA throughout the cerebral cortex indicated that NCAN production involves developing neurons as well as other cell populations, including radial glial cells (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the widespread distribution of Ncan mRNA shown in Figure 2a.

claim: NCAN protein densely accumulates in cell-sparse zones such as the SP/IZ and MZ.
source: In contrast to Ncan mRNA, NCAN protein densely accumulated in cell-sparse zones, such as the SP/IZ and marginal zone (MZ), but was less abundant in cell-dense regions, such as the CP and VZ (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: NCAN protein is less abundant in cell-dense regions such as the CP and VZ.
source: In contrast to Ncan mRNA, NCAN protein densely accumulated in cell-sparse zones, such as the SP/IZ and marginal zone (MZ), but was less abundant in cell-dense regions, such as the CP and VZ (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There is a discrepancy between Ncan mRNA and NCAN protein distribution patterns.
source: This discrepancy in the Ncan mRNA and NCAN protein distribution pattern suggested a mechanism through which secreted NCAN protein localizes to the SP/IZ and MZ.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the distribution patterns of mRNA (Figure 2a) and protein (Figure 2b).

claim: A mechanism exists through which secreted NCAN protein localizes to the SP/IZ and MZ.
source: This discrepancy in the Ncan mRNA and NCAN protein distribution pattern suggested a mechanism through which secreted NCAN protein localizes to the SP/IZ and MZ.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observed discrepancy between mRNA and protein distribution.

claim: The localization pattern of NCAN is similar to that of HA.
source: We noticed that the localization pattern of NCAN was similar to that of HA, which we previously reported (Figure 2c; Takechi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing immunohistochemical data in Figure 2b and 2c, and cited previous work by Takechi et al., 2020.

claim: NCAN and HA co-localize in cortical neuronal cultures as punctate signals at adhesion sites between the neuron and culture substrate.
source: Furthermore, NCAN and HA co-localized in cortical neuronal cultures as punctate signals at adhesion sites between the neuron and culture substrate, indicating that NCAN formed a pericellular matrix with HA (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: NCAN forms a pericellular matrix with HA.
source: Furthermore, NCAN and HA co-localized in cortical neuronal cultures as punctate signals at adhesion sites between the neuron and culture substrate, indicating that NCAN formed a pericellular matrix with HA (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-localization data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: NCAN interacts with endogenous HA.
source: This analysis confirmed the interaction between NCAN and endogenous HA (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The precipitation of NCAN depends on intact HA.
source: The precipitation of NCAN depended on intact HA because NCAN disappeared from precipitates by digestion with hyaluronidase from Streptomyces hyalurolyticus, which specifically degrades HA and does not act on other glycosaminoglycans (Ohya and Kaneko, 1970).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of NCAN precipitation after hyaluronidase treatment, and cited methodology from Ohya and Kaneko, 1970.

claim: Exogenously added biotinylated HA binds to the N-terminal portion of NCAN.
source: In addition, exogenously added biotinylated HA (b-HA) is also bound to the N-terminal portion of NCAN (Figure 2g).
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Full-length and N-terminal half of NCAN precipitate a larger amount of HA than the C-terminal half.
source: Quantification of HA by ELISA demonstrated that the full-length and N-terminal half of NCAN precipitated a larger amount of HA than the C-terminal half (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), supporting the binding between the N-terminal portion of NCAN and HA.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The N-terminal portion of NCAN binds to HA.
source: Quantification of HA by ELISA demonstrated that the full-length and N-terminal half of NCAN precipitated a larger amount of HA than the C-terminal half (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), supporting the binding between the N-terminal portion of NCAN and HA.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: TNC exhibits specific binding to NCAN.
source: Among the identified proteins, only TNC exhibited specific binding to NCAN.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS analysis results presented in Table 1.

claim: The C-terminal half, but not the N-terminal half of NCAN, binds to TNC.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation followed by immunoblot analysis showed that the C-terminal half, but not the N-terminal half of NCAN, is bound to TNC (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Interactions between NCAN and TNC are dependent on a divalent cation.
source: Interactions between NCAN and TNC were dependent on a divalent cation but not on chondroitin sulfate chains on NCAN consistent with previous findings (Aspberg et al., 1997; Rauch et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and cited previous findings from Aspberg et al., 1997 and Rauch et al., 1997.

claim: Interactions between NCAN and TNC are not dependent on chondroitin sulfate chains on NCAN.
source: Interactions between NCAN and TNC were dependent on a divalent cation but not on chondroitin sulfate chains on NCAN consistent with previous findings (Aspberg et al., 1997; Rauch et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and cited previous findings from Aspberg et al., 1997 and Rauch et al., 1997.

claim: TNC expression at mRNA and protein levels peaks during late embryonic brain development.
source: The expression of TNC at mRNA and protein levels peaked during late embryonic brain development, similar to the expression pattern of NCAN (Figure 3c–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR and immunoblot data shown in Figures 3c-e.

claim: Tnc mRNA is confined to the VZ where the cell bodies of radial glial cells reside in the developing cerebral cortex at E16.5.
source: In situ hybridization analysis indicated that in the developing cerebral cortex at E16.5, Tnc mRNA was confined to the VZ where the cell bodies of radial glia cells reside (Figure 3f), consistent with previous findings (Faissner et al., 2017; Garcion et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3f and cited previous findings from Faissner et al., 2017 and Garcion et al., 2004.

claim: Radial glial cells are the primary source of TNC in earlier developmental stages.
source: While some astrocytes express TNC during gliogenesis (E18 or later), it has been documented that radial glial cells are the primary source of TNC in earlier stages (Faissner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Faissner et al., 2017.

claim: TNC protein is observed in the SP/IZ and MZ, similar to the localization of NCAN.
source: However, TNC protein was not restricted to the VZ but was also observed in the SP/IZ and MZ, similar to the localization of NCAN (Figure 3g).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: A C-type lectin domain (CLD) of NCAN interacts with the 4th and 5th fibronectin type-III domains (FNIII) of TNC.
source: In this modeled complex, a C-type lectin domain (CLD) of NCAN interacts with the 4th and 5th fibronectin type-III domains (FNIII) of TNC, which is consistent with a previously reported structure of aggrecan (ACAN) and tenascin-R (TNR; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b; Lundell et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by AlphaFold2 multimer analysis and cited previous structural data from Lundell et al., 2004.

claim: Amino acid residues in the interface of NCAN-TNC and ACAN-TNR complex are highly conserved.
source: Amino acid residues in the interface of NCAN-TNC and ACAN-TNR complex were highly conserved (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figures 4c and 4d.

claim: An Asn residue (Asn1148 in mNCAN and Asn2022 in rACAN), which interacts with Ca2+ ions, is conserved.
source: An Asn residue (Asn1148 in mNCAN and Asn2022 in rACAN), which interacts with Ca2+ ions, was also conserved.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The amino acid residues in FNIII-4 involved in the binding to NCAN are not well conserved among other FNIII domains of TNC.
source: Sequence alignments of fourteen FNIII of TNC indicated that the amino acid residues in FNIII-4 involved in the binding to NCAN are not well conserved among other FNIII (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: NCAN derived from developing neurons and radial glial cells binds to multiple sites on a long chain of HA via the N-terminal Link modules.
source: From these results, we proposed that NCAN, HA, and TNC cooperatively assemble a supramolecular complex as follows: (1) NCAN derived from developing neurons and radial glial cells binds to multiple sites on a long chain of HA via the N-terminal Link modules; (2) The hexamer of TNC secreted from radial glial cells cross-links NCAN through the interaction between the FNIII-4 domain of TNC and the CLD of NCAN (Figure 4e).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the combined experimental data.

claim: The hexamer of TNC secreted from radial glial cells cross-links NCAN through the interaction between the FNIII-4 domain of TNC and the CLD of NCAN.
source: From these results, we proposed that NCAN, HA, and TNC cooperatively assemble a supramolecular complex as follows: (1) NCAN derived from developing neurons and radial glial cells binds to multiple sites on a long chain of HA via the N-terminal Link modules; (2) The hexamer of TNC secreted from radial glial cells cross-links NCAN through the interaction between the FNIII-4 domain of TNC and the CLD of NCAN (Figure 4e).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the combined experimental data.

claim: HA, NCAN, and TNC co-localize in the upper part of the SP/IZ and MZ of the developing cerebral cortex at E17.5.
source: HA, NCAN, and TNC were co-localized in the upper part of the SP/IZ and MZ of the developing cerebral cortex at E17.5 (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by triple immunostaining data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: HA, NCAN, and TNC show aggregate-like deposition in the SP/IZ.
source: High-magnification views showed the aggregate-like deposition of these molecules in the SP/IZ (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-magnification imaging data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Co-localization of HA, NCAN, and TNC is rarely observed in the CP or VZ.
source: Co-localization of these three molecules was rarely observed in the CP or VZ.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the imaging data showing predominant co-localization in SP/IZ.

claim: The ternary complex of HA, NCAN, and TNC frequently contacts the surface of migrating neurons.
source: Z-stack projections of confocal images revealed that the ternary complex frequently contacted the surface of migrating neurons (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figures 5c and 5d.

claim: The ternary complex is deposited extracellularly surrounding the cell body and neurites of bipolar neurons.
source: Orthogonal views of 3D images showed the extracellular deposition of the ternary complex surrounding the cell body and neurites of bipolar neurons (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data shown in Figures 5c and 5d.

claim: Neither TNC nor NCAN is detected in DKO mice.
source: Neither TNC nor NCAN was detected in the DKO mice, and the brain weights were not different compared to wild-type (WT) mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Brain weights are not different between DKO and WT mice.
source: Neither TNC nor NCAN was detected in the DKO mice, and the brain weights were not different compared to wild-type (WT) mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by brain weight measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the lateral cortex of WT mice, many labeled cells are migrating in the upper and lower SP/IZ, and a smaller population has already reached the CP at E16.5.
source: In the lateral cortex of WT mice, many labeled cells were migrating in the upper and lower SP/IZ, and a smaller population had already reached the CP (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by Flash Tag labeling data shown in Figures 6a and 6b.

claim: In DKO mice, most cells reside beneath the lower SP/IZ, and very few reach the upper SP/IZ and CP at E16.5.
source: In DKO mice, most cells resided beneath the lower SP/IZ, and very few reached the upper SP/IZ and CP.
evidence: The claim is supported by Flash Tag labeling data shown in Figures 6a and 6b.

claim: DKO mice have a significantly lower percentage of labeled cells in the upper layers (Bin 1 and 2) and more cells in the lower layers (Bin 4 and 5) than WT mice in the lateral cortex at E16.5.
source: Bin analysis showed that DKO mice had a significantly lower percentage of labeled cells in the upper layers (Bin 1 and 2) and more cells in the lower layers (Bin 4 and 5) than WT mice (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative bin analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: In the medial cortex of WT mice, neurons reach the CP more quickly than in the lateral cortex.
source: In the medial cortex of WT mice, neurons reached the CP more quickly than in the lateral cortex (Figure 6c; Yoshinaga et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by Flash Tag labeling data shown in Figure 6c and cited previous findings from Yoshinaga et al., 2021.

claim: DKO mice exhibit slower neuronal migration in the medial cortex than WT mice.
source: DKO mice exhibited slower neuronal migration in the medial cortex than WT mice, suggesting that the ternary complex facilitated the entry of neurons into the CP in a wide range of cortical regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by Flash Tag labeling data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The ternary complex facilitates the entry of neurons into the CP in a wide range of cortical regions.
source: DKO mice exhibited slower neuronal migration in the medial cortex than WT mice, suggesting that the ternary complex facilitated the entry of neurons into the CP in a wide range of cortical regions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of delayed migration in DKO mice across different cortical regions.

claim: Delayed migration in DKO mice is mostly restored after 3 days of labeling.
source: However, delayed migration in DKO mice was mostly restored after 3 days of labeling (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: The claim is supported by Flash Tag labeling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a, b.

claim: No notable abnormalities are observed in the laminar structure of DKO mice at 2 weeks of age.
source: No notable abnormalities were observed in the laminar structure of DKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 3a, b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3a, b.

claim: The laminar distribution of Ctip2-positive deep layer neurons shows no significant differences between WT and DKO mice at 2 weeks of age.
source: Additionally, the laminar distribution of Ctip2-positive deep layer neurons showed no significant differences between WT and DKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 3a, c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3a, c.

claim: While the ternary complex is necessary for proper neuronal migration, some compensatory mechanisms may mitigate its effects in the postnatal brain.
source: These results suggest that while the ternary complex is necessary for proper neuronal migration, some compensatory mechanisms may mitigate its effects in the postnatal brain.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observation that migration defects are transient.

claim: The loss of NCAN and TNC does not affect the number of Pax6-positive radial glial cells and Tbr2-positive intermediate progenitor cells.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis showed no significant differences between WT and DKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4a.

claim: The morphology of nestin-positive radial fibers is indistinguishable between WT and DKO mice.
source: Additionally, the morphology of nestin-positive radial fibers was indistinguishable between WT and DKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 4b, c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4b, c.

claim: The delay in neuronal migration in DKO mice is not due to decreased proliferation of radial glial cells.
source: These results suggested that the delay in neuronal migration was not due to the decreased proliferation of radial glial cells in DKO mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that progenitor cell numbers are unchanged in DKO mice.

claim: NCAN KO mice have a significantly lower percentage of labeled cells in the upper layer (Bin2) and more cells in the lower layer (Bin5) than WT mice at E16.5.
source: In NCAN KO mice, a significantly lower percentage of labeled cells resided in the upper layer (Bin2), and more cells remained in the lower layer (Bin5) than in WT mice (Figure 7a).
evidence: The claim is supported by Flash Tag labeling data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The impact of a single deletion of TNC on neuronal cell migration is very limited.
source: In contrast, the impact of a single deletion of TNC on neuronal cell migration was very limited.
evidence: The claim is supported by Flash Tag labeling data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: TNC KO mice exhibit a tendency to have a higher proportion of labeled cells in the lower layer (Bin4) than WT mice, but this does not reach statistical significance.
source: Although TNC KO mice exhibited a tendency to have a higher proportion of labeled cells in the lower layer (Bin4) than in WT mice, this did not reach statistical significance (Figure 7a).
evidence: The claim is supported by Flash Tag labeling data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The delay in neuronal migration observed in single KO mice is milder compared to DKO mice.
source: The delay in neuronal migration observed in the single KO mice was milder when compared to that observed in DKO mice (Figure 6a–c), suggesting that simultaneous deletion of both NCAN and TNC is necessary for a more pronounced impairment in neuronal cell migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing Flash Tag labeling data from Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Simultaneous deletion of both NCAN and TNC is necessary for a more pronounced impairment in neuronal cell migration.
source: The delay in neuronal migration observed in the single KO mice was milder when compared to that observed in DKO mice (Figure 6a–c), suggesting that simultaneous deletion of both NCAN and TNC is necessary for a more pronounced impairment in neuronal cell migration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the severity of migration defects in single vs. double KO mice.

claim: In NCAN KO mice, the localization of TNC shifts to the lower layers compared to WT mice.
source: In WT mice, TNC was accumulated in the SP/IZ, whereas in NCAN KO mice, the localization of TNC shifted to the lower layers (Figure 7b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: TNC KO mice exhibit an attenuated accumulation of NCAN in the SP/IZ compared with WT mice.
source: Furthermore, TNC KO mice exhibited an attenuated accumulation of NCAN in the SP/IZ compared with WT mice (Figure 7c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: TNC and NCAN are mutually required for their localization in the SP/IZ.
source: These results suggest that TNC and NCAN are mutually required for their localization in the SP/IZ.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that loss of one component affects the localization of the other.

claim: Expression of GFP-fused NCAN increases the accumulation of TNC in NCAN KO mice.
source: Immunostaining of TNC around the transfected Turbo-RFP-positive neurons after 2 days indicated that expression of GFP-fused NCAN increased the accumulation of TNC compared to controls (Figure 7e and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figures 7e and 7f.

claim: TNC is localized adjacent to GFP-fused NCAN.
source: Higher magnification views showed that TNC was localized adjacent to GFP-fused NCAN (Figure 7g).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-magnification imaging data shown in Figure 7g.

claim: In DKO mice, the accumulation of HA is decreased in the SP/IZ.
source: Additionally, in DKO mice, the accumulation of HA, another component of the ternary complex, was also decreased in the SP/IZ (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The reduction in HA accumulation is less pronounced in single KO mice compared to DKO mice.
source: The reduction in HA accumulation was less pronounced in single KO mice compared to DKO mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b), indicating that HA could not localize in the SP/IZ only when both NCAN and TNC were absent.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b.

claim: HA cannot localize in the SP/IZ only when both NCAN and TNC are absent.
source: The reduction in HA accumulation was less pronounced in single KO mice compared to DKO mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b), indicating that HA could not localize in the SP/IZ only when both NCAN and TNC were absent.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing HA accumulation in single vs. double KO mice.

claim: The majority of HA disappears from the cerebral cortex 2 days after hyaluronidase injection.
source: The majority of HA disappeared from the cerebral cortex 2 days after the injection (Figure 8a).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: The staining intensity of NCAN and TNC significantly decreases at the SP/IZ following hyaluronidase treatment.
source: We noted that the staining intensity of NCAN and TNC significantly decreased at the SP/IZ following the hyaluronidase treatment, indicating the interaction of these molecules and the requirement of HA for the localization of NCAN and TNC.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: HA is required for the localization of NCAN and TNC.
source: We noted that the staining intensity of NCAN and TNC significantly decreased at the SP/IZ following the hyaluronidase treatment, indicating the interaction of these molecules and the requirement of HA for the localization of NCAN and TNC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that HA degradation reduces NCAN and TNC localization.

claim: Digestion of HA reduces the amount of NCAN and TNC in the cerebral cortex by approximately half.
source: Immunoblot analysis showed that the digestion of HA reduced the amount of NCAN and TNC in the cerebral cortex by approximately half, confirming the essential role of HA in the retention of NCAN and TNC (Figure 8b and c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 8b and 8c.

claim: HA plays an essential role in the retention of NCAN and TNC.
source: Immunoblot analysis showed that the digestion of HA reduced the amount of NCAN and TNC in the cerebral cortex by approximately half, confirming the essential role of HA in the retention of NCAN and TNC (Figure 8b and c).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that HA degradation reduces NCAN and TNC levels.

claim: Hyaluronidase injection at E14.5 inhibits neuronal migration into the CP in the lateral and medial cortices.
source: Migration assay using Flash Tag showed that in comparisons with PBS-injected controls, a hyaluronidase injection at E14.5 inhibited neuronal migration into the CP in the lateral and medial cortices (Figure 8d and e).
evidence: The claim is supported by Flash Tag labeling data shown in Figures 8d and 8e.

claim: The impact of hyaluronidase treatment on neuronal migration is not as prominent as observed in DKO mice.
source: However, the impact of hyaluronidase treatment on neuronal migration was not as prominent as observed in DKO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing migration data from hyaluronidase-treated mice and DKO mice.

claim: Approximately half of NCAN and TNC remain in the tissue after hyaluronidase digestion.
source: This result could be attributed to the fact that approximately half of NCAN and TNC remained in the tissue after hyaluronidase digestion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the immunoblot data showing partial reduction of NCAN and TNC after hyaluronidase treatment.

claim: DKO mice show a significantly lower length-to-width ratio of neurons than WT mice at 53 hours after in utero electroporation.
source: Morphological analysis revealed a significantly lower length-to-width ratio of neurons in DKO mice than in WT mice (Figure 9c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figures 9c and 9d.

claim: Control neurons have an elongated shape, whereas neurons in DKO mice retain a rounded shape.
source: This result indicated that control neurons had an elongated shape, whereas neurons in DKO mice retained a rounded shape.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the length-to-width ratio data.

claim: Many neurons in WT mice radially extend their major neurites toward the pia surface (between 70° and 90° relative to the ventricle surface).
source: Many neurons radially extended their major neurites toward the pia surface (between 70° and 90° relative to the ventricle surface) in WT mice, which is characteristic of bipolar neurons (Figure 9e).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 9e.

claim: The major neurites of DKO neurons are not directed toward the pia surface compared to control neurons.
source: Compared with control neurons, the major neurites of DKO neurons were not directed toward the pia surface.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 9e.

claim: A significantly smaller proportion of bipolar neurons is observed in DKO mice than in WT mice.
source: Consistent with these results, we observed a significantly smaller proportion of bipolar neurons in DKO mice than in WT mice (Figure 9f).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis data shown in Figure 9f.

claim: Retarded neuronal migration in DKO mice is associated with defects in the multipolar-to-bipolar transition.
source: Therefore, retarded neuronal migration in DKO mice was associated with defects in the multipolar-to-bipolar transition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined morphological and migration data.

claim: Culturing neurons on TNC-coated plates significantly accelerates neurite outgrowth after 2 days of plating.
source: After 2 days of plating, culturing neurons on the TNC-coated plates significantly accelerated neurite outgrowth (Figure 10c).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 10c.

claim: The length of the longest neurite notably increases when the glass plate is coated with 10 μg/mL of TNC.
source: The length of the longest neurite notably increased when the glass plate was coated with 10 μg/mL of TNC (Figure 10d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative neurite length data shown in Figure 10d.

claim: Coating with 10 μg/mL of HA or NCAN does not significantly affect neurite elongation.
source: In contrast, coating with 10 μg/mL of HA or NCAN did not significantly affect neurite elongation.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative neurite length data shown in Figure 10d.

claim: Plating neurons on TNC increases the total length and number of neurites.
source: Plating neurons on TNC also increased the total length and number of neurites (Figure 10e and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative neurite analysis data shown in Figures 10e and 10f.

claim: The effect of TNC on neurite outgrowth is evident after 3 days of plating.
source: This effect of TNC on neurite outgrowth was also evident after 3 days of plating (Figure 10—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1a–d.

claim: TNC enhances the morphological transition of cortical neurons from stages 1 to 3 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Closer observations found that TNC enhances the morphological transition of cortical neurons from stages 1 to 3 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 10g), suggesting that TNC stimulates the multipolar-to-bipolar transition.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological stage analysis data shown in Figure 10g.

claim: TNC stimulates the multipolar-to-bipolar transition.
source: Closer observations found that TNC enhances the morphological transition of cortical neurons from stages 1 to 3 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 10g), suggesting that TNC stimulates the multipolar-to-bipolar transition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TNC promotes morphological maturation.

claim: NCAN KO neurons exhibit significantly suppressed elongation of the longest neurite compared to WT neurons after 2 days of plating.
source: After 2 and 3 days of plating, NCAN KO neurons exhibited a significantly suppressed elongation of the longest neurite compared to WT neurons (Figure 10h and i, Figure 10—figure supplement 3a, b).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative neurite length data shown in Figures 10h, 10i, and Figure 10—figure supplement 3a, b.

claim: The deletion of NCAN reduces the total length and number of neurites.
source: Additionally, the deletion of NCAN reduced the total length and number of neurites (Figure 10j and k, Figure 10—figure supplement 3c, d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative neurite analysis data shown in Figures 10j, 10k, and Figure 10—figure supplement 3c, d.

claim: TNC and NCAN play critical roles in the morphological maturation of cortical neurons.
source: These results indicated that TNC and NCAN play critical roles in the morphological maturation of cortical neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined in vitro culture data showing effects of TNC and NCAN on neurite outgrowth.

claim: The multipolar-to-bipolar transition is a critical step in establishing neuronal polarity.
source: The multipolar-to-bipolar transition is a critical step in establishing neuronal polarity.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cortical development.

claim: Defects in the multipolar-to-bipolar transition lead to neuronal mispositioning, laminar structure disorganization, and cortical development malformation.
source: Defects in the multipolar-to-bipolar transition lead to neuronal mispositioning, laminar structure disorganization, and cortical development malformation (Castello and Gleeson, 2021; Fernández et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Castello and Gleeson, 2021 and Fernández et al., 2016.

claim: The assembly of ECM molecules in the SP/IZ provides an extracellular positional cue for migrating neurons that specify the site of the multipolar-to-bipolar transition.
source: The present results propose that the assembly of ECM molecules in the SP/IZ provides an extracellular positional cue for migrating neurons that specify the site of the multipolar-to-bipolar transition.
evidence: The claim is a proposed interpretation based on the combined experimental results.

claim: Polarity formation in vivo occurs in a microenvironment or niche created in the SP/IZ.
source: Polarity formation in vivo occurs in a microenvironment or niche created in the SP/IZ.
evidence: The claim is a proposed interpretation based on the experimental results.

claim: A gradient of semaphorin 3A in the developing cerebral cortex regulates neuronal migration and polarity by attracting apical dendrites and repulsing axons.
source: A gradient of semaphorin 3 A in the developing cerebral cortex regulates neuronal migration and polarity by attracting apical dendrites and repulsing axons (Chen et al., 2008; Polleux et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Chen et al., 2008 and Polleux et al., 2000.

claim: Transforming growth factor-β initiates signaling pathways that specify axons.
source: Transforming growth factor-β initiates signaling pathways that specify axons (Yi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Yi et al., 2010.

claim: Reelin is essential for completing neuronal migration and cortical lamination.
source: Reelin, a glycoprotein secreted by Cajal-Retzius cells in the MZ, is essential for completing neuronal migration and cortical lamination (D'Arcangelo et al., 1995; Jossin and Cooper, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from D'Arcangelo et al., 1995 and Jossin and Cooper, 2011.

claim: A combination of ECM molecules, secreted factors, and neighboring cells regulates neuronal polarity during cortical development.
source: Therefore, a combination of ECM molecules, secreted factors, and neighboring cells regulates neuronal polarity during cortical development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the discussion of multiple factors affecting neuronal polarity.

claim: Radial glial cells secrete and deposit TNC to stimulate the morphological transition of migrating neurons in the SP/IZ.
source: The present study discovered another role for radial glial cells: they secrete and deposit TNC to stimulate the morphological transition of migrating neurons in the SP/IZ.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined experimental results.

claim: Basal/outer radial glial cells generate the majority of cortical neurons in gyrencephalic species such as humans.
source: In gyrencephalic species, such as humans, basal/outer radial glial cells residing in the outer sub-VZ generate the majority of cortical neurons and are responsible for the expansion of the cerebral cortex (Kriegstein and Alvarez-Buylla, 2009; Taverna et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Kriegstein and Alvarez-Buylla, 2009 and Taverna et al., 2014.

claim: Basal/outer radial glial cells are characterized by high gene expression of several ECM molecules, including TNC.
source: Basal/outer radial glial cells are characterized by the high gene expression of several ECM molecules, including TNC (Fietz et al., 2012; Pollen et al., 2015), indicating that basal/outer radial glial cells create a microenvironment that promotes neuronal migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Fietz et al., 2012 and Pollen et al., 2015.

claim: Basal/outer radial glial cells create a microenvironment that promotes neuronal migration.
source: Basal/outer radial glial cells are characterized by the high gene expression of several ECM molecules, including TNC (Fietz et al., 2012; Pollen et al., 2015), indicating that basal/outer radial glial cells create a microenvironment that promotes neuronal migration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of high ECM expression in basal/outer radial glial cells.

claim: HA-based ECM affects the cortical folding of the developing human neocortex.
source: In addition, HA-based ECM affects the cortical folding of the developing human neocortex (Long et al., 2018), suggesting that the evolutionarily conserved ECM structure contributes to neocortex expansion in gyrencephalic species.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Long et al., 2018.

claim: The evolutionarily conserved ECM structure contributes to neocortex expansion in gyrencephalic species.
source: In addition, HA-based ECM affects the cortical folding of the developing human neocortex (Long et al., 2018), suggesting that the evolutionarily conserved ECM structure contributes to neocortex expansion in gyrencephalic species.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observation of HA-based ECM effects on cortical folding.

claim: Alternatively spliced FNIIIs of TNC stimulate neurite outgrowth by binding to neuronal surface contactin-1 in primary cultured neurons.
source: For example, alternatively spliced FNIIIs stimulate neurite outgrowth by binding to neuronal surface contactin-1 in primary cultured neurons (Rigato et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Rigato et al., 2002.

claim: Several integrins have been identified as receptors for TNC.
source: Several integrins have been identified as receptors for TNC, and through this interaction, TNC influences cell adhesion, migration, and proliferation (Tucker and Chiquet-Ehrismann, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Tucker and Chiquet-Ehrismann, 2015.

claim: TNC influences cell adhesion, migration, and proliferation through interaction with integrins.
source: Several integrins have been identified as receptors for TNC, and through this interaction, TNC influences cell adhesion, migration, and proliferation (Tucker and Chiquet-Ehrismann, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Tucker and Chiquet-Ehrismann, 2015.

claim: Binding to HA via NCAN is required for the deposition of TNC in the SP/IZ.
source: Our analysis revealed that binding to HA via NCAN was required for the deposition of TNC in the SP/IZ.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined experimental results.

claim: The expression of NCAN and TNC is high in the embryonic brain.
source: The expression of NCAN and TNC is high in the embryonic brain, whereas ACAN, brevican, and TNR increase during late postnatal development.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about developmental ECM transitions.

claim: ACAN, brevican, and TNR increase during late postnatal development.
source: The expression of NCAN and TNC is high in the embryonic brain, whereas ACAN, brevican, and TNR increase during late postnatal development.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about developmental ECM transitions.

claim: In the adult brain, ACAN cross-links HA and TNR and forms macromolecular aggregates around subpopulations of neurons.
source: In the adult brain, ACAN cross-links HA and TNR and forms macromolecular aggregates around subpopulations of neurons (Fawcett et al., 2022; Miyata and Kitagawa, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Fawcett et al., 2022 and Miyata and Kitagawa, 2017.

claim: Perineuronal nets are formed at late postnatal stages and play pivotal roles in neural plasticity, memory consolidation, and circuit maturation.
source: This condensed ECM structure, called perineuronal nets, is formed at the late postnatal stages and plays pivotal roles in neural plasticity, memory consolidation, and circuit maturation (Fawcett et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Fawcett et al., 2022.

claim: The ternary complex of ACAN, HA, and TNR physically stabilizes existing synapses and inhibits new synapse formation.
source: The ternary complex of ACAN, HA, and TNR physically stabilizes existing synapses and inhibits new synapse formation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about perineuronal net function.

claim: High-molecular-weight HA serves as a structural scaffold in perineuronal nets, facilitating the accumulation of ECM around subpopulations of neurons in the adult brain.
source: In perineuronal nets, high-molecular-weight HA serves as a structural scaffold, facilitating the accumulation of ECM around subpopulations of neurons in the adult brain.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about perineuronal net structure.

claim: A structurally similar ternary complex of NCAN, HA, and TNC is formed in the SP/IZ of the embryonic cortex but exerts distinct functions in cortical development.
source: The present study showed that a structurally similar ternary complex of NCAN, HA, and TNC was formed in the SP/IZ of the embryonic cortex but exerted distinct functions in cortical development.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined experimental results.

claim: NCAN and TNC are upregulated in reactive astrocytes.
source: Previous studies have reported an upregulation of NCAN and TNC in reactive astrocytes, indicating the potential formation of the ternary complex of NCAN, TNC, and HA in the adult brain in response to injury (Deller et al., 1997; Haas et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Deller et al., 1997 and Haas et al., 1999.

claim: The ternary complex of NCAN, TNC, and HA may form in the adult brain in response to injury.
source: Previous studies have reported an upregulation of NCAN and TNC in reactive astrocytes, indicating the potential formation of the ternary complex of NCAN, TNC, and HA in the adult brain in response to injury (Deller et al., 1997; Haas et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observation of NCAN and TNC upregulation in reactive astrocytes.

claim: The enzymatic digestion of HA impedes the accumulation of NCAN and TNC within the SP/IZ.
source: The enzymatic digestion of HA impedes the accumulation of NCAN and TNC within the SP/IZ, supporting that HA functions as a scaffold for ECM in the developing brain.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced NCAN and TNC accumulation after HA digestion.

claim: HA functions as a scaffold for ECM in the developing brain.
source: The enzymatic digestion of HA impedes the accumulation of NCAN and TNC within the SP/IZ, supporting that HA functions as a scaffold for ECM in the developing brain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that HA digestion reduces NCAN and TNC accumulation.

claim: HA may transmit extracellular signals to developing neurons through cell surface HA receptors such as CD44.
source: Alternatively, HA may transmit extracellular signals to developing neurons through cell surface HA receptors such as CD44 (Skupien et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is speculated based on cited previous findings from Skupien et al., 2014.

claim: The interaction of NCAN with HA and TNC was previously reported in vitro.
source: Although the interaction of NCAN with HA and TNC was previously reported in vitro, the present results revealed the formation of the ternary complex in vivo for the first time.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from previous in vitro studies.

claim: The present results revealed the formation of the ternary complex of NCAN, HA, and TNC in vivo for the first time.
source: Although the interaction of NCAN with HA and TNC was previously reported in vitro, the present results revealed the formation of the ternary complex in vivo for the first time.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined experimental results.

claim: Full-length NCAN is detected during early development but not in adulthood.
source: Full-length NCAN is detected during early development but not in adulthood, indicating that the proteolytic cleavage of NCAN affects the assembly of the ternary complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data showing developmental changes in NCAN forms.

claim: The proteolytic cleavage of NCAN affects the assembly of the ternary complex.
source: Full-length NCAN is detected during early development but not in adulthood, indicating that the proteolytic cleavage of NCAN affects the assembly of the ternary complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of developmental changes in NCAN forms.

claim: Matrix metalloprotease-2 cleaves the central region of NCAN in vitro.
source: Screening using peptide library mixtures revealed that matrix metalloprotease-2 cleaved the central region of NCAN in vitro (Turk et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Turk et al., 2001.

claim: The temporal control of matrix metalloproteases may affect neuronal migration via the assembly and disassembly of the ECM.
source: The temporal control of matrix metalloproteases may affect neuronal migration via the assembly and disassembly of the ECM.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the known role of matrix metalloproteases in ECM remodeling.

claim: Single deletion of NCAN leads to mild abnormalities in neuronal migration.
source: We observed that single deletion of NCAN leads to mild abnormalities in neuronal migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by Flash Tag labeling data from NCAN KO mice.

claim: The loss of NCAN may interfere with TNC localization and thus delay neuronal migration.
source: The loss of NCAN may interfere with TNC localization and thus delay neuronal migration.
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observation that NCAN KO affects TNC localization.

claim: The binding of NCAN to cell adhesion molecules on the neuronal surfaces may affect neurite outgrowth.
source: Alternatively, the binding of NCAN to cell adhesion molecules on the neuronal surfaces may affect neurite outgrowth (Friedlander et al., 1994; Rauch et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is speculated based on cited previous findings from Friedlander et al., 1994 and Rauch et al., 2001.

claim: Genetic variation in NCAN is a risk factor for bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.
source: Genome-wide association studies identified a genetic variation in NCAN as a risk factor for bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from genome-wide association studies.

claim: The relationship between delayed neuronal migration in NCAN KO mice and the onset of neuropsychiatric disorders remains uncertain.
source: However, the relationship between the delayed neuronal migration observed in NCAN KO mice and the onset of neuropsychiatric disorders remains uncertain.
evidence: The claim acknowledges the uncertainty in linking the observed phenotype to disease.

claim: In adult NCAN KO mice, there are no apparent deficits in brain anatomy, morphology, or ultrastructure.
source: In adult NCAN KO mice, there are no apparent deficits in brain anatomy, morphology, or ultrastructure (Zhou et al., 2001), which is consistent with our results that the delay in neuronal migration in DKO mice is transient.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous findings from Zhou et al., 2001.

claim: The C-terminal portion of NCAN promotes synapse formation during postnatal development.
source: A recent study reported that the C-terminal portion of NCAN promotes synapse formation during postnatal development, which may be more relevant to neuropsychiatric disorders (Irala et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited recent findings from Irala et al., 2023.

claim: NCAN has different functions in the embryonic and adult brain.
source: These findings suggest that NCAN has different functions in the embryonic and adult brain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the discussion of NCAN's roles at different developmental stages.

claim: The assembly of NCAN, HA, and TNC forms the microenvironment in the SP/IZ, in which the multipolar-to-bipolar transition occurs.
source: In conclusion, the present study revealed that the assembly of NCAN, HA, and TNC forms the microenvironment in the SP/IZ, in which the multipolar-to-bipolar transition occurs.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined experimental results.

claim: Enzymatic and genetic disruption of the ternary complex impairs radial migration by inhibiting the multipolar-to-bipolar transition.
source: We uncovered that enzymatic and genetic disruption of the ternary complex impairs radial migration by inhibiting the multipolar-to-bipolar transition.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined experimental results.

claim: The findings shed light on the collaborative role of ECM molecules derived from neurons and radial glial cells in cortical development.
source: Our findings shed light on the collaborative role of ECM molecules derived from neurons and radial glial cells in cortical development.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined experimental results.
